qs.q: Evaluate \[ \int_1^\infty \frac{\ln x}{x}\,dx. \]
hints: This is an improper integral with an infinite limit, so write it as a limit.
Replace the upper limit by $b$, find an antiderivative with a substitution, then let $b\to\infty$.
$\int_a^\infty f\,dx=\lim_{b\to\infty}\int_a^b f\,dx$; the integral converges only if this limit is finite. Also $\int u\,du=\tfrac{u^2}{2}+C$.
steps: As $b\to\infty$, $\dfrac{(\ln b)^2}{2}\to\infty$, so the integral diverges.

qs.q: Evaluate \[ \int_3^6 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}. \]
hints: The integrand is unbounded at an endpoint, so this is an improper integral of the second type.
Find the antiderivative (an inverse sine) and replace the bad endpoint by a limit.
$\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=\arcsin\dfrac xa+C$, and for an infinite discontinuity at $b$: $\int_a^b f=\lim_{t\to b^-}\int_a^t f$.
steps: The integrand is infinite at $x=6$; an antiderivative is $\arcsin\dfrac x6$.

qs.q: The sequence whose $n$th term is $a_n=\dfrac{\cos 2n}{3^n}$ converges to:
hints: Cosine is bounded, while the denominator grows, so try the squeeze theorem.
Bound $|a_n|$ above and below using $-1\le\cos 2n\le1$.
Squeeze theorem: if $b_n\le a_n\le c_n$ and $b_n\to L$, $c_n\to L$, then $a_n\to L$; also $r^n\to0$ for $|r|<1$.
qs.brief: $|a_n|\le(1/3)^n\to0$, so by squeeze the limit is $0$.

qs.q: Find the sum \[ \sum_{n=0}^\infty\left(-\frac15\right)^n+\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{(2n+1)(2n+3)}. \]
hints: One series is geometric and the other telescopes after partial fractions.
Sum the geometric series with its ratio, and split the second term into two fractions to see the cancellation.
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty ar^n=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ for $|r|<1$, and $\dfrac{1}{(2n+1)(2n+3)}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1{2n+1}-\dfrac1{2n+3}\right)$.

qs.q: Which one of the following series is/are convergent? \[ \text{(I) } \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{n}{n^4+2n^2+1}\qquad \text{(II) } \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{n^{1.001}}\qquad \text{(III) } \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n^{0.9}} \]
hints: Compare each series with a $p$-series.
For (I), compare the dominant powers of $n$ in the numerator and denominator; for (II) and (III) read off $p$.
The $p$-series $\sum 1/n^p$ converges iff $p>1$; the limit comparison test works when $a_n/b_n\to L$ with $0<L<\infty$.
steps: (I) behaves like $\dfrac{n}{n^4}=\dfrac1{n^3}$ ($p=3>1$); limit comparison with $\sum 1/n^3$ gives a finite positive limit, so it converges.
So only I and II converge.
qs.brief: I $\sim1/n^3$ converges, II ($p=1.001$) converges, III ($p=0.9$) diverges.

qs.q: Which one of the following series is/are divergent? \[ \text{(I) } \sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin\frac1n\qquad \text{(II) } \sum_{n=1}^\infty e^{-n^2}\qquad \text{(III) } \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{5}{4^n+1} \]
hints: Use comparison tests, comparing each series with a familiar one.
For (I) use limit comparison with the harmonic series; for (II) and (III) bound the terms by a geometric series.
Limit comparison: if $a_n/b_n\to L$ with $0<L<\infty$, both series behave alike; $\sum r^n$ converges iff $|r|<1$; $\sin u/u\to1$ as $u\to0$.
steps: (II) $e^{-n^2}\le e^{-n}=(1/e)^n$, a convergent geometric series, so (II) converges.
qs.brief: I diverges (limit comparison with $\sum1/n$); II and III converge (geometric bounds).

qs.q: Using the Remainder Theorem, the least number of terms required to approximate the sum of the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ with an error of less than $0.02$ is:
hints: This is an alternating series, so use the alternating series remainder estimate.
Require the first omitted term to be less than $0.02$ and solve for the number of terms.
For a convergent alternating series, $|S-S_N|\le a_{N+1}$, the first omitted term.
steps: The least number of terms is $7$.

qs.q: The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt n}$
opts: diverges by the Alternating Series Test
hints: Test the series itself and the series of absolute values separately.
Apply the alternating series test, then check $\sum|a_n|$ as a $p$-series.

Alternating series test: $b_n$ decreasing with $b_n\to0$ gives convergence of $\sum(-1)^nb_n$; the $p$-series $\sum1/n^p$ converges iff $p>1$; converging but not absolutely means conditional convergence.
steps: $b_n=\dfrac1{\sqrt n}$ is decreasing and tends to $0$, so the series converges.
qs.brief: Alternating series test passes, but $\sum n^{-1/2}$ diverges: conditional convergence.

qs.q: Which one of the following series is/are divergent? \[ \text{(I) } \sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{6^n}{(n+1)^3}\qquad \text{(II) } \sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(n!)^2}{(3n)!}\qquad \text{(III) } \sum_{n=1}^\infty\left(\frac{-3n}{2n+1}\right)^{3n} \]
hints: Use the ratio test for (I) and (II) and the root test for (III).
Compute $\lim|a_{n+1}/a_n|$ for the first two and $\lim|a_n|^{1/n}$ for the third.
If $L=\lim|a_{n+1}/a_n|$ (or $\lim|a_n|^{1/n}$), the series converges for $L<1$ and diverges for $L>1$.
qs.brief: Ratio: I gives $6>1$, II gives $0$; root: III gives $27/8>1$. I and III diverge.

qs.q: If a Taylor polynomial for $f(x)=\sqrt x$ centered at $c=4$ is written in the form $p_2(x)=a_2x^2+a_1x+a_0$, then $64a_2+8a_1+4a_0=$
hints: Build the degree-2 Taylor polynomial at the given center.
Compute $f(4)$, $f'(4)$, $f''(4)$, write $p_2$ in powers of $(x-4)$, then expand and read off the coefficients.
$p_2(x)=f(c)+f'(c)(x-c)+\dfrac{f''(c)}{2}(x-c)^2$; expand $(x-c)^2=x^2-2cx+c^2$ to collect the coefficients.

qs.q: The series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n\,n!\,(x-5)^n}{3^n}$ converges
hints: This is a power series, so find its radius of convergence with the ratio test.
Form $\left|\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|$ and see what happens to the factorial as $n\to\infty$.
A power series $\sum c_n(x-a)^n$ always converges at $x=a$; if $\lim|a_{n+1}/a_n|=\infty$ for every $x\ne a$, the radius of convergence is $0$.
steps: For $x\ne5$ this tends to $\infty>1$, so the series diverges.
At $x=5$ every term with $n\ge1$ is $0$, so it converges. The series converges only at $x=5$.

qs.q: A power series representation for the function $f(x)=\dfrac{3x-1}{x^2-1}$ centered at $c=0$ is:
hints: Split the function by partial fractions and use geometric series.
Write $f(x)=\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x+1}$ and turn each piece into the form $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$\dfrac1{1-r}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty r^n$ for $|r|<1$, so $\dfrac1{1-x}=\sum x^n$ and $\dfrac1{1+x}=\sum(-1)^nx^n$.

qs.q: The coefficient of $x^7$ in the Maclaurin series for the function $f(x)=\sinh x$ is:
hints: Use the Maclaurin series of $\sinh x$ or the coefficient formula.
Note that the derivatives of $\sinh x$ alternate between $\cosh x$ and $\sinh x$, and evaluate them at $0$.
The coefficient of $x^k$ in a Maclaurin series is $\dfrac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}$.
steps: The derivatives alternate $\sinh x,\cosh x,\sinh x,\dots$ so $f^{(k)}(0)=0$ for even $k$ and $1$ for odd $k$.

qs.q: $\int\frac{\cos\theta}{\sqrt{1-\sin\theta}}\,d\theta=$
hints: The numerator is related to the derivative of the expression inside the root, so use substitution.
Let $u$ be the expression under the square root and find $du$.
$\int u^{-1/2}\,du=2u^{1/2}+C$, and $d(1-\sin\theta)=-\cos\theta\,d\theta$.

qs.q: $\int\frac{4}{x^2\sqrt{4+x^2}}\,dx=$
hints: The expression $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ suggests a trigonometric substitution.
Substitute $x=2\tan\theta$ and simplify the square root and $dx$.
For $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ use $x=a\tan\theta$, giving $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}=a\sec\theta$ and $dx=a\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$; also $\int\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}d\theta=-\csc\theta+C$.
steps: From the triangle, $\csc\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{4+x^2}}{x}$, so the result is $-\dfrac{\sqrt{4+x^2}}{x}+C$.

qs.q: $\int\frac{\tan^3x}{\sqrt{\sec x}}\,dx=$
hints: This is an integral of powers of tangent and secant.
Split off $\sec x\tan x$ so that $u=\sec x$ works, and rewrite the rest with $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$.
$\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sec x=\sec x\tan x$.
steps: Write $\dfrac{\tan^3x}{\sqrt{\sec x}}=\dfrac{\tan^2x}{(\sec x)^{3/2}}\,\sec x\tan x=\dfrac{\sec^2x-1}{(\sec x)^{3/2}}\,\sec x\tan x$.
So the result is $\dfrac23(\sec x)^{3/2}+2(\sec x)^{-1/2}+C$.

qs.q: The volume of the solid generated by revolving the region bounded by the graphs of $y=e^{-x}$, $y=0$, $x=0$, and $x=1$ about the $x$-axis is:
hints: Revolving about the $x$-axis a region that touches the axis gives disks.
Set up $\pi\int(\text{radius})^2dx$ with radius $e^{-x}$ over $[0,1]$.
Disk method: $V=\pi\int_a^b[f(x)]^2\,dx$, and $\int e^{kx}dx=\dfrac{e^{kx}}k+C$.

qs.q: The area of the region bounded by the graphs of the equations $y=12-x^2$, $y=x$, $x=-1$ and $x=1$ is:
hints: Area between two curves: decide which curve is on top.
Compare $12-x^2$ and $x$ on $[-1,1]$, then integrate top minus bottom.
$A=\int_a^b\left[f(x)-g(x)\right]dx$ when $f\ge g$ on $[a,b]$.
steps: On $[-1,1]$: $12-x^2\ge11>x$, so the parabola is on top.

qs.q: The arc length of the graph of the function $f(x)=\dfrac13x^{3/2}-1$ over the interval $[2,6]$ is:
hints: Use the arc length formula with the derivative of $f$.
Compute $f'(x)$, then simplify $1+(f')^2$ to a linear expression under the root.
$L=\int_a^b\sqrt{1+\left[f'(x)\right]^2}\,dx$, and $\int\sqrt{u}\,du=\dfrac23u^{3/2}+C$.

qs.q: $\int x\sec^2x\,dx=$
hints: The integrand is a product of a polynomial and a function with a known antiderivative, so use integration by parts.
Choose $u=x$ and $dv=\sec^2x\,dx$.
$\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$, $\int\sec^2x\,dx=\tan x+C$, and $\int\tan x\,dx=-\ln|\cos x|+C$.
